title: Revisiting Thermal Scalability for Large-Scale Superconducting Quantum Systems
authors: Shaswot Shresthamali, Ilkwon Byun, Teruo Tanimoto, Yoshinori Uzawa, Kunihiro Inomata, Tsuyoshi Yamamoto, Koji Inoue
abstract: The readout amplification chain imposes a critical thermal scalability bottleneck in large-scale superconducting quantum systems. This happens through three mechanisms: amplifier dissipation, passive conduction through bias wiring and Joule heating within that same wiring. These terms are absent or only partially represented in several prior system-level thermal-scalability models, leading to bottleneck misidentification and scalability overestimation. In this work, we improve upon previous system-level heat estimation models by fully accounting for the major heat sources in modern cryogenic quantum systems including the active dissipation, passive conduction, and Joule heating in the readout amplifier module. Our analysis demonstrates that amplifier-associated heat emerges as the dominant thermal bottleneck that fundamentally alters the thermal landscape of modern large-scale cryogenic systems. We explore various technology options and their tradeoffs to identify configurations that reduce this critical heat load and improve scalability. Finally, we evaluate forward-looking system configurations, including larger refrigeration platforms and optical approaches, and analyze forward-looking pathways toward single-fridge 10k-qubit cryogenic systems.
summary: This paper revisits the thermal limits of superconducting quantum computers by developing an advanced heat estimation model. It demonstrates that previously overlooked heat sources, particularly from readout amplifiers and wiring resistance, create a dominant thermal bottleneck. The findings are critical for designing viable, large-scale cryogenic quantum hardware.
main_problem: The readout amplification chain imposes a critical thermal scalability bottleneck that limits the size of superconducting quantum processors.
main_result: Amplifier-associated heat emerges as the dominant thermal bottleneck in modern large-scale cryogenic systems, requiring new modeling approaches to predict true qubit capacity.
method: The authors developed an improved system-level thermal estimation model that fully accounts for active dissipation, passive conduction, and Joule heating across multiple cryogenic stages.
model_or_system: The study models superconducting quantum processors housed in a dilution refrigerator (DR) with distinct temperature stages ($	ext{RT}$ down to $\sim 10	ext{ mK}$). The model calculates the total normalized heat load by summing contributions from cables, attenuators, and amplifiers.
key_observables: Total Normalized Heat Load ($	ext{NHL}_{	ext{THL},s}$) at each cryogenic stage; maximum supported physical qubit capacity.
important_parameters: Active dissipation, passive conduction coefficients, Joule heating resistance/currents, target scale (e.g., 10k qubits).
main_assumptions: Previous models are criticized for omitting or underestimating the combined heat load from the readout amplifier chain, leading to overestimation of scalability.

paper_structure: The paper introduces the thermal bottleneck problem, details the improved unified modeling framework incorporating all major heat sources, analyzes cross-technology trade-offs, and concludes by evaluating pathways toward large single-fridge systems.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware limitations in scaling quantum computation, which is crucial for any theoretical physicist working on open quantum systems or building complex quantum architectures.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Simplified schematic of the cryogenic system in [8] consisting of the dilution refrigerator that houses the quantum processor and the supporting infrastructure. The major heat loads arise from heat conduction via the metallic cables (passive heat loads), heat dissipation through attenuators and amplifiers (active heat loads), and Joule heating (ohmic heat loads). Components with negligible heat footprint (e.g., circulators, filters, isolators) are not shown for simplicity.

FIGURE 2. Normalized heat loads at different temperature stages under two wiring assumptions for the system in [8]. (left) Reproduced scalability trend for the stainless-steel wiring architecture considered in [8]. In this case, the millikelvin stages dominate because stainless-steel drive and flux-bias cables introduce large passive and ohmic heat loads. (right) Hypothetical replacement of stainless-steel cables with Cri/oFlex wiring [12] and upgrading the fridge to KIDE. Higher-capacity refrigeration and lower-PHL cabling increase the qubit count, but more importantly they change the scaling trend and shift the dominant bottleneck toward the 4 K stage. FIGURE 3. Active heat dissipation in attenuators along the DRIVE line during a single-qubit (1Q) operation. Each attenuator is assumed to dissipate all incident power as heat (pessimistic estimation). The DRIVE line has a total attenuation of 60 dB, distributed across multiple temperature stages. A 1Q operation requires −71 dBm of average power delivered to the qubit at the MXC [8]. The input power at each attenuator at different temperature stages along the drive line is obtained by propagating this value upstream from the MXC stage. As a result, the control signals generated at RT require an average power of −11 dBm.
